questions.q: According to the Census of India, what is the minimum population threshold for a city to be classified as a "Million-Plus City" or "Metropolitan City"?
questions.a: The minimum population threshold is 1 million (10 lakh) as per the Census of India. A wrong answer (e.g., 5 lakh or 50 lakh) reveals the student confuses Class I town threshold (1 lakh) with metropolitan threshold, or confuses "metro" with "megacity" (10 million+). This indicates inability to apply the specific Census classification hierarchy.

questions.q: Why does the Census of India use "Urban Agglomeration" (UA) rather than "Municipal Corporation" boundaries when classifying metropolitan cities?
questions.a: Urban Agglomeration includes the core city plus contiguous outgrowths (railway colonies, university campuses, port areas) and adjoining towns that form a continuous urban spread, capturing the true functional urban extent. Municipal boundaries often exclude rapidly growing peri-urban areas. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks administrative boundaries equal functional urban areas, missing the geographical concept of "continuous built-up area" critical for metropolitan analysis.

questions.q: Using the 2011 Census data, identify which state has the highest number of million-plus cities and calculate what percentage of India's total million-plus cities it contains. (Total million-plus cities in India 2011: 53)
questions.a: Step 1: Recall 2011 Census - Maharashtra has 7 million-plus cities (Greater Mumbai, Pune, Nagpur, Nashik, Vasai-Virar, Aurangabad, Solapur). Step 2: Total million-plus cities = 53. Step 3: Percentage = (7/53) × 100 = 13.2%. A wrong answer (e.g., Uttar Pradesh or Tamil Nadu) reveals the student cannot recall the state-wise distribution pattern or misapplies total city count. This tests both factual recall and quantitative geographical skill.

questions.q: Compare the spatial distribution of million-plus cities in the Northern Plains versus the Peninsular Plateau. What geographical factors explain the difference in density and clustering?
questions.a: Northern Plains: High density linear clustering along Ganga-Yamuna corridor (Delhi, Meerut, Kanpur, Lucknow, Prayagraj, Varanasi, Patna) due to fertile alluvial soil, dense river network, historical trade routes, and flat terrain enabling transport. Peninsular Plateau: Dispersed, isolated metropolitan nodes (Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai) due to rugged terrain, scattered mineral/industrial resources, and historical princely state capitals. A wrong answer listing only "population" or "industrialisation" misses the physical geography template (relief, soil, drainage) that pre-conditions urban location.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The emergence of new million-plus cities in Kerala (Kochi, Kozhikode, Thrissur, Malappuram, Kannur, Kollam) between 2001-2011 represents genuine urbanisation rather than statistical reclassification." Support your judgment with geographical evidence.
questions.a: This is largely statistical reclassification, not genuine urbanisation. Evidence: Kerala's urbanisation is characterised by "rural-urban continuum" - high density rural areas with non-agricultural employment. The 2011 Census redefined "urban" to include Census Towns (population >5000, density >400/km², >75% male non-agricultural workers). Kerala added 36 Census Towns in 2011. True metropolitan functions (corporate HQs, specialised services, transport hubs) remain concentrated in Kochi/Thiruvananthapuram. A wrong evaluation accepting the statement at face value shows inability to distinguish between demographic threshold crossing and functional metropolitan transformation.

questions.q: Design a thematic map annotation scheme to show the hierarchical relationship between India's 7 megacities (10 million+), 53 million-plus cities, and 468 Class I towns (1 lakh+) using 2011 Census data. Specify symbols, colours, and label hierarchy.
questions.a: Good answer: Use proportional circles - Megacities: Red circle (radius ∝ log population), bold label with UA name. Million-plus (non-mega): Orange circle, medium label. Class I towns: Yellow dot, small label. Inset: Pie chart showing state-wise share. Colour gradient from red→orange→yellow shows hierarchy. Poor answer: Uses same symbol for all, or only maps megacities, missing the hierarchical urban system concept. This reveals inability to translate quantitative Census hierarchy into cartographic representation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A Metropolitan City in India is an urban agglomeration with a population of 1 million (10 lakh) or more as per the Census of India, functioning as a major economic, administrative, and cultural hub with significant ______ development and regional influence.
Fill in the blank: Look at a map of India at night - the brightest clusters are Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, ______, Hyderabad.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can classify Indian cities using Census population thresholds, map the spatial distribution of million-plus cities across states, explain the functional differences between metropolitan cities and other urban centres, and analyse the relationship between metropolitan growth and regional development disparities using Census.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Look at a map of India at night - the ______ clusters are Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad.
